MSK–SKIN · MEDICAL COLLEGE OF GEORGIA · LECTURE COMPANION

Common Hand Problems

A region-first clinical anatomy guide: structure → mechanism → examination finding → management, grounded in Dr. Mark Fulcher’s lecture.

103-slide source8 teaching sectionsOriginal lecture imagery

Learning objectives · derived from the lecture

The provided slide deck does not list a separate formal objective slide; these objectives reflect its teaching outline.

  1. Localize key hand and wrist structures, movements and sensory regions used in the lecture.
  2. Distinguish DIP mucous cyst, paronychia, felon and herpetic whitlow by anatomy and management.
  3. Explain A1 pulley trigger finger and differentiate it from flexor sheath infection using Kanavel’s signs.
  4. Connect Dupuytren fibroproliferation, contractures, the tabletop test and management options.
  5. Recognize median neuropathy at the carpal tunnel and distinguish common radial thumb/wrist diagnoses.

Big picture

A painful hand complaint is often solved by where the abnormality sits: nail fold vs pulp, flexor sheath vs A1 pulley, palmar aponeurosis vs median nerve, and thumb CMC joint vs first dorsal compartment. Localization then predicts the exam maneuver and urgent management distinctions.

COMMON HAND PROBLEMS

01 · Anatomy review & the regional map

Dr. Fulcher begins with the skeleton, soft-tissue anatomy, sensory fields and movements because the location of a symptom is often the first diagnostic clue. The clinical lecture then moves from distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint → metacarpophalangeal (MP/MCP) joint → palm → wrist.

RegionLandmarks and processes emphasized
DIP / fingertipJoint, nail matrix, nail fold, pulp space
MP/MCPA1 pulley, flexor tendon sheath
PalmPalmar aponeurosis, median nerve at carpal tunnel
Wrist / thumb baseFirst CMC, first dorsal compartment, ganglion origins
MUST KNOW
Distinguish thumb palmar abduction from radial abduction, and finger abduction/adduction from the middle-finger axis. This makes the later provocative tests and tendon findings meaningful.
COMMON HAND PROBLEMS

02 · Digital nerve block & distal fingertip conditions

Digital nerve block

The lecture demonstrates a digital block using a 27-gauge needle and lists plain 1% lidocaine and plain 0.5% bupivacaine. The goal is anesthesia across the finger’s digital nerve distribution; the slide photographs show the palmar and dorsal extent. These are the lecturer’s listed agents, not a complete procedural protocol.

Mucous cyst of the DIP joint

In the lecture, DIP joint arthritis leads to a ganglion/mucous cyst. The nearby osteophytes and nail matrix explain why a dorsal DIP mass may cause pain, clear mucinous drainage, and longitudinal nail grooving. The lecture lists observation, aspiration and osteophyte debridement as management options.

CLINICAL CONNECTION
An apparently superficial bump can arise from deeper DIP degenerative change. A change in nail contour is an anatomic localization clue, not a separate nail disease.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why might a DIP mucous cyst produce longitudinal nail grooving?

The cyst lies close to the nail matrix; pressure on the matrix changes nail formation.

COMMON HAND PROBLEMS

03 · Fingertip infections: location dictates treatment

Dr. Fulcher places paronychia, felon, and herpetic whitlow together because they may all produce distal digit pain, but the involved compartment and whether drainage is appropriate differ.

DiagnosisWhere?Key lecture finding / treatment distinction
ParonychiaNail foldEarly: antibiotics; established: incision and drainage. The lecturer notes that part or all of the nail plate may require removal for decompression.
FelonDistal pulp spaceEarly: antibiotics; established: incision and drainage.
Herpetic whitlowHSV infection of digitDo NOT debride—critical distinction from bacterial abscesses.
EXAM TRAP
Do not manage every painful, swollen fingertip as a bacterial collection: herpetic whitlow is caused by HSV and should not be incised or debrided.
BOARD / CLINICAL ENRICHMENT
Herpetic whitlow typically produces grouped vesicles and may be preceded by burning/tingling. This morphology helps distinguish it from a felon.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Patient with painful fingertip swelling: which anatomic clue separates paronychia from felon?

Paronychia centers on the nail fold; a felon involves the volar pulp compartment.

COMMON HAND PROBLEMS

04 · Trigger finger: stenosing tendovaginitis at A1

Trigger finger is described as stenosing tendovaginitis at the A1 pulley near the transverse palmar/MP flexion crease. A tendon that fails to glide smoothly through the pulley produces catching, locking, and sometimes an inability to make a fist.

ExaminationMechanistic explanation
Tender over A1Stenosis/friction occurs where the flexor tendon enters the pulley.
Palpable triggeringTendon movement intermittently catches at the narrowed passage.
Cannot fully close fistPain/catching interferes with normal flexor excursion.

Management in the lecture: steroid injection (quoted as 80% effective) and surgical A1 release (described as highly successful).

COMMON CONFUSION
Trigger finger = mechanical catching near A1; Dupuytren contracture = progressive fascial cord that holds the digit flexed. One involves the flexor tendon pulley; the other involves palmar fascia.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why does A1 pulley disease produce a finger that locks?

Tendon gliding is obstructed at a narrowed pulley; finger motion causes catching rather than smooth excursion.

COMMON HAND PROBLEMS

05 · Purulent flexor tenosynovitis: one of the hand emergencies

An infection within a digit’s flexor tendon sheath can threaten tendon gliding and function. The lecturer highlights penetration injuries, especially involving the index, long, and ring fingers, and teaches Kanavel’s four cardinal signs.

1Digit held in flexion
2Circumferential swelling
3Tenderness along sheath
4Pain with passive extension

Timing matters in this lecture: “early” disease (<24 hours) → antibiotics and close follow-up; “established” disease (>24–48 hours) → drainage. The professor emphasizes this is one of the few emergencies.

MUST KNOW
Memorize all four Kanavel signs and recognize this as a time-sensitive surgical evaluation problem, not routine trigger finger.
BOARD / CLINICAL ENRICHMENT
Passive extension stretches an inflamed flexor tendon sheath, explaining the characteristic pain. Suspected pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis warrants urgent hand-surgery assessment.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which presentation specifically suggests an infected flexor sheath rather than trigger finger?

A swollen, resting-flexed digit with sheath tenderness and especially pain on passive extension (Kanavel signs).

COMMON HAND PROBLEMS

06 · Dupuytren contracture: palmar fascia becomes a cord

Dupuytren disease is a fibroproliferative disease of the hand. A nodule in the palm progresses to a cord; contractile myofibroblasts and predominantly type III collagen in cords contribute to flexion contracture. The professor contrasts this with type I collagen in normal palmar fascia.

The lecture describes predominance in the ring and small fingers, MP and PIP contractures, an often nonpainful presentation, northern European ancestry associations, autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance, and diathesis (younger onset, aggressive disease). Its chromosome 16q association is presented as uncertain (“?”).

Function and treatment threshold

Contractures can interfere with washing the face, combing hair, putting a hand in a pocket, glove use, golf or racquet sports. The lecture uses the tabletop test and cites treatment for MP/PIP contracture >20°. The examples classify a hand unable to lay flat as requiring hand-surgeon consultation.

Management taught: collagenase (Xiaflex) injection, fasciotomy or fasciectomy. Lecture images show injection into a cord, manipulation approximately 36 hours later, cord rupture and restored extension. The lecture notes quicker recovery but greater recurrence with collagenase compared with surgery.

COMMON CONFUSION
Dupuytren cord is palmar fascia, not the flexor tendon. A patient may have fixed flexion contracture without painful A1 triggering.
LECTURE → STEP 1 BRIDGE
Myofibroblast contraction + collagen-rich fascia → progressive cord → MP/PIP flexion contracture → positive tabletop test.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · What is the tissue abnormality in Dupuytren, and why is it different from trigger finger?

Palmar aponeurosis fibroproliferation forms contractile cords; trigger finger is tendon/pulley stenosis at A1.

COMMON HAND PROBLEMS

07 · Carpal tunnel: median nerve compression at the wrist

The carpal tunnel is bounded by the carpal arch (bones) and the transverse carpal ligament/flexor retinaculum. The median nerve travels within it alongside the digital flexor tendons. Compression causes characteristic sensory symptoms and can eventually impair thenar function.

Classic symptoms from the lecture: median distribution numbness/tingling, worse at night or while driving, and relief by shaking out the hand. Examine for thenar atrophy, Phalen test, Tinel sign and altered two-point discrimination.

Lecture managementPoint to remember
ConservativeNSAIDs, splints (effective), steroid injection in early symptoms
SurgicalCarpal tunnel release; lecturer quotes 95% good-to-excellent results and says it may be curative
FIRST AID CONNECTION
The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve travels superficial to the flexor retinaculum, so central palm sensation can be spared in carpal tunnel syndrome. The median nerve and nine flexor tendons pass inside the tunnel.
EXAM TRAP
CTS = median compression at the wrist; Guyon canal = ulnar nerve/artery. Thenar atrophy supports severe median involvement, while loss of finger interosseous function points toward an ulnar lesion.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why is the palm often spared in a classic CTS sensory examination?

The median palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the carpal tunnel and passes outside it.

COMMON HAND PROBLEMS

08 · Painful thumb base & wrist masses

First CMC osteoarthritis

The first carpometacarpal joint is critical for thumb motion and pinch. The lecture emphasizes women more often than men, typical onset in the sixth–seventh decades, and activity-related aching at the base of the thumb. Examination uses the CMC grind test; the lecturer identifies a Bett’s view radiograph.

Management in lecture: NSAIDs, splinting, steroid injections, or surgery (arthroplasty with ligament reconstruction tendon interposition [LRTI] or arthrodesis).

De Quervain disease

First dorsal compartment stenosing tenosynovitis involves the abductor pollicis longus (APL) and extensor pollicis brevis (EPB). The examination localizes tenderness to the radial styloid and uses Finkelstein’s test. The lecture explicitly says to rule out first CMC arthrosis before committing to the diagnosis.

Management: NSAIDs, thumb-spica splint, steroid injection, and release if indicated.

Ganglion cysts

The lecture calls ganglia the most common soft-tissue mass of the hand, with mucinous contents. Dorsal (60–70%) ganglia usually arise from the scapholunate joint; volar (~20%) ganglia occur near the FCR–APL interval and often originate from the radiocarpal or scaphotrapezoid joint.

The lecturer lists observation, the historical “Bible treatment,” aspiration (questioned as about 50% success), and surgical excision. The Bible treatment is mentioned as lecture history, not a recommendation for self-treatment.

DiagnosisWhat localizes it?Distinguishing feature
First CMC OAJoint at thumb baseActivity ache; positive grind
De QuervainRadial styloid, first dorsal compartmentAPL/EPB; Finkelstein
Dorsal ganglionPosterior wrist, scapholunate regionMucinous cystic mass
Volar ganglionAnterior radial wrist, FCR/APL intervalAssociated with radiocarpal/scaphotrapezoid joint
MSK CONNECTION
These diagnoses overlap anatomically, but the precise site of tenderness and the provocative test identify whether the problem is first CMC cartilage, first dorsal compartment tendon glide, or a cystic joint-associated mass.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Radial wrist pain: what distinguishes first CMC arthritis from de Quervain disease?

CMC arthritis localizes to the thumb-base joint and is provoked by grind; de Quervain localizes over the radial styloid/APL–EPB compartment and is provoked by Finkelstein testing.

MASTER THESE BEFORE MOVING ON

  1. Diagnosis follows anatomic compartment. Nail fold, pulp, flexor sheath, pulley and palmar fascia produce different patterns.
  2. Trigger finger ≠ Dupuytren. A1 stenosis causes catching; fascia cords cause fixed contracture.
  3. Kanavel signs identify urgent sheath infection. All four findings and the need for prompt assessment matter.
  4. Median nerve at carpal tunnel. Nocturnal median-distribution symptoms and thenar atrophy connect nerve compression to function.
  5. Radial thumb/wrist differential. CMC grind versus Finkelstein versus cystic mass separates three commonly confused diagnoses.

THE MOST USEFUL FIRST AID CONNECTIONS

  1. Carpal tunnel: median nerve + nine tendons; palmar cutaneous median branch is spared.
  2. Purulent flexor tenosynovitis: sheath infection → pain with passive extension (mechanism of Kanavel sign).
  3. De Quervain: first dorsal compartment APL + EPB.
  4. Dupuytren: palmar fascia/myofibroblasts → fibrous cords → contracture.

Course source: Mark Fulcher, MD, Common Hand Problems, Medical College of Georgia, 103-slide PDF. Selective outside points are explicitly labeled. Lecture-specific treatment claims reflect the slides, not a current clinical practice guideline.
